name: Testing a Tutor Before Students Use It
title: Testing a Tutor Before Students Use It
answer: Testing a tutor before students use it means a teacher tries to break the setup by acting like a struggling student, asking for answers and making mistakes. The test also checks whether the tutor's explanations are accurate. It matters because a short test can prevent problems that would otherwise affect a whole class.

sections.body: Every tutor configured for a school should be tested before any student uses it. A teacher can take the role of a struggling student, request answers directly, make common mistakes, and try to get the tool to do the work. If the tutor gives in, the setup needs more work. The test takes half an hour and can prevent problems that could affect a whole class. Testing also looks for errors in the tool's own knowledge by asking it to explain the lesson's key ideas and checking those explanations for accuracy.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not give separate steps by grade band, so the same approach applies wherever a tutor is configured. A teacher first plays a struggling student and tries to get the tool to give answers or do the work. The teacher then asks the tutor to explain the lesson's key ideas and checks the explanations for accuracy. A short trial with a few students before full use can catch problems that simulations missed. The results are written down as a short note of what was tested, what went wrong, and what was changed.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports research on a carefully designed math tutor found that real classroom use revealed problems that computer simulations had missed (Looi et al., 2026). It also states that a short trial with a few students before full use can catch those problems too. The text does not give an evidence label for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The decisions stay with a person. A teacher must judge whether the tutor gives in, whether its explanations are accurate, and what changes are needed. The text says if the tool gives in, the setup needs more work. Testing does not remove the need for a short trial with a few students before full use. The written note of what was tested, what went wrong, and what was changed helps the next teacher and builds a district set of tested setups that teachers can reuse.
